newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to keep options open on Thomson - Jospin.
newsitem.headline: France to keep options open on Thomson - Jospin.

text.p: The new French government will be guided solely by the national interest in deciding its policy on defence electronics company Thomson-CSF, Socialist Prime Minster Lionel Jospin said on Saturday.

The previous conservative government last year launched the sale of the state's 58 percent stake in Thomson-CSF but lost power three weeks ago to the Socialists, whose election campaign was hostile to privatisations.

"As I have indicated in my declaration on general policy, these issues will be examined with the sole measure of national interest, without taboos or excluding anything, without of course being trapped by pre-established schemes, and with the concern of moving closer to other European partners," Jospin said in a speech at the Paris air show.
"In the electronics sector, whose importance has only grown since the fall of the Berlin Wall and still more since the Gulf War, we have to nurture our technological potential.
"By its size and capabilities, Thomson-CSF represents a vital resource and an indisputable centre of excellence to meet these challenges," Jospin said.
He said he was aware of the expectations on the key issues in the industry but he would only talk about them after a detailed study of all the options.

Jospin gave a keynote address to parliament last Thursday, in which he said he did not favour state selloffs, unless national interests demanded it, but did not want to stop French state firms from striking partnerships with other European companies.

European and U.S. aerospace executives have been anxious to know the government's plans for Thomson-CSF and a merger also launched last year between state-owned Aerospatiale and combat plane maker Dassault Aviation.

The Thomson-CSF privatisation and the Aerospatiale-Dassault merger were seen as keys to unlock further European defence consolidation, needed to face up to competition from mega-merger in the United States.
French telecommunications giant Alcatel Alsthom and the Lagardere group had put in rival bids for Thomson-CSF.
